# Isaiah 3: Verse-by-verse research notes

**About the sources.** I ran out of search and fetch requests before I could cover every tradition, so some sections below are thin or missing:
- **Read in full:** Enduring Word (Guzik) and Ellicott (whole chapter).
- **Read in part, through search-result pages:** Gill, Calvin, Matthew Henry, Barnes, Pulpit Commentary, JFB, Benson, Wesley, Coffman, Cambridge Bible, Keil & Delitzsch, Preceptaustin, Bible.org (Utley) and Biblical Illustrator.
- **Not found at all:** anything from Lutheran, Pentecostal (other than Guzik), Catholic or Orthodox teachers, or from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers. I've left those out rather than guess.

---

### v. 1
- **Divine titles.** Guzik says "Lord" translates *adonai* (master) and "LORD" translates *Yahweh*. "LORD of hosts" pictures God as commander of heaven's armies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-3/
- **"Supply and support."** Ellicott says the text explains these as the two basics of life, bread and water. He also suggests that explanation may be a later note added to the text, and that the "supports" may really be the "pillars of the state" listed next. Since v. 7 implies famine, Isaiah may mean both kinds of collapse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-3.html

### vv. 2–3
- **Traditional reading.** Guzik: God judges by removing competent leaders at every level. He sees the fulfilment in 2 Kings 24:14 and a lasting principle that God can judge a nation with incompetent, ungodly leaders. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-3/
- **Babylon or Rome?** Gill (Baptist) argues this can't mean the Babylonian captivity, because Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Daniel were prophesying then. He takes it as the Roman destruction of Jerusalem. https://studylight.org/commentaries/geb/isaiah-3.html Benson and Barnes instead tie it to Nebuchadnezzar and Jehoiachin's captivity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/3-2.htm
- **"Diviner/soothsayer": disputed.**
  - Calvin (Reformed) thinks the word is used here in a good sense, for someone with unusual insight, since Isaiah is listing what keeps a nation in good order. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/3-2.html
  - JFB takes it in the bad sense: the diviners the people trusted will let them down. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/3-2.htm
  - Coffman says listing them doesn't mean Isaiah thought their powers were real. It shows how far gone the nation was, treating such people as its main supports. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/3-2.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary says Isaiah lists the classes in the order the people valued them, not the order he did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/3-2.htm
- **"Captain of fifty."** JFB: not just commanders of thousands and hundreds, but even officers over fifty men will be gone. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Isa/Isa_003.cfm
- **"Skilled craftsman."** Ellicott notes that 2 Kings 24:14 groups craftsmen with the mighty men taken to Babylon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-3.html

### v. 4
- Calvin: "children" means childish in mind and conduct, not only in age: weak, foolish rulers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/3-4.html
- Ellicott suggests a hint at Ahaz, who became king at twenty, and mentions Manasseh (twelve) and Josiah (eight). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-3.html
- Barnes (citing Lowth) sees it fulfilled in the line of weak kings down to Zedekiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/3-4.html

### v. 5
- Guzik: bad leadership leads to social breakdown. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-3/
- Ellicott: chaos, a fierce struggle to survive, and the young mocking the experience of the old. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-3.html

### vv. 6–7
- Guzik: owning a decent cloak becomes enough to qualify someone to lead, and even that man refuses. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-3/
- Ellicott: the refusal shows a "save yourself" selfishness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-3.html
- Henry: he takes an oath that he cannot carry the cost of the office. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/3-3.html

### v. 8
- Guzik: they sin by what they say as well as what they do, citing Matthew 12:36–37. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-3/
- Ellicott: the nation's outward troubles are traced to their real source, offending God's glorious presence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-3.html

### v. 9
- Guzik: their sin is shameless. He argues that keeping outward decency matters, and that holding up a standard you don't perfectly meet is not hypocrisy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-3/
- Ellicott sees the Sodom comparison as mainly about luxury and loose living (Ezekiel 16:49), possibly with a more specific likeness as well. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-3.html

### vv. 10–11
- **Traditional reading.** Henry: God tells the prophets to comfort the righteous, who will not be lost among the crowd of sinners (Genesis 18:25). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/3-10.html Calvin agrees: even when disaster falls on good and bad alike, God still tells them apart. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/3-10.html
- **Not a promise of no suffering.** Preceptaustin: God promises it will "go well," not that the righteous will escape suffering. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_310-12_commentary Abernethy (Biblical Illustrator) says it does not promise outward prosperity in this world. https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/3-10.htm
- **Works and grace.** JFB says this is salvation by a faith that bears fruit, not by works. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/3-10.htm A Biblical Illustrator sermon says eating the fruit of our own deeds is the old-covenant basis, and Christians rest on the fruit of Christ's doings. https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/3-10.htm
- **Spurgeon on v. 11.** Quoted by Guzik: don't let present appearances make you doubt that it will go badly for the wicked. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-3/
- **Modern scholarship.** The Cambridge Bible notes that some scholars think vv. 10–11 were added later and fit loosely in context. It also says a small change to the Hebrew consonants gives "Happy is the righteous!" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/3-10.htm
- **Greek text (Septuagint).** It reads quite differently: "Let us bind the righteous, for he is troublesome to us." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/3-10.htm

### v. 12 (the main verse where readings differ)
- **"Women rule over them" is a curse for society.** Guzik (Calvary Chapel) grants that God raised up individual women such as Deborah and Esther. But he says a society where women generally rule is "cursed, not blessed." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-3/ Bible Hub's study notes appeal to 1 Timothy 2:12–13 and God's intention of male leadership, while saying the verse shows moral disorder, not that women are inferior. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/3-12.htm
- **It's figurative, about weak men.**
  - Wesley (Methodist): "weak and effeminate rulers." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/3-12.html
  - Barnes: not literal. It means either rulers under the influence of the royal harem, or rulers lacking vigour. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/3-12.html
  - Coffman: the verse is not a put-down of women but a metaphor for the rulers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/3-12.html
- **Historical readings.** Ellicott points to Ahaz and the queen-mother's influence in his counsels. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-3.html Gill offers several options, including later Herodian women. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/3-12.html
- **Different Hebrew reading.** The NET Bible translates "creditors rule over them." https://www.blueletterbible.org/sample/net/isa/3/1/ Utley (Bible.org) explains that the TEV, NJB and REB follow the Septuagint, changing "women" to "creditors." https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-3 Clarke similarly suggests "usurers" in place of "women." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/isaiah/3-12.html
- **"Guides mislead you."** JFB says the Hebrew word means "those who call you blessed": false prophets who flatter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/3-12.htm The Catholic Douay-Rheims translation reads it the same way. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/3-12.htm This is a translation only; I found no Catholic commentary on it.

### v. 13
- Guzik: the LORD is both prosecutor and judge, so a guilty verdict is certain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-3/
- Ellicott: the people may think the prophet is their critic, but God is their real accuser. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-3.html

### vv. 14–15
- Guzik: the charge is not merely failing to help the poor, but actively robbing them to get rich. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-3/
- JFB: the "vineyard" is the Jewish nation under God's rule (compare Isaiah 5:1–7). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Isa/Isa_003.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary draws out God's care for the poor and links it to Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/isaiah-3.html

### v. 16
- **Who they are.** Henry: the wives and daughters of the princes who oppressed the poor to pay for their families' luxury. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_003.cfm Gill agrees on who they were and calls pride the root of it all. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/3-16.html
- **Was immorality involved? Commentators split.**
  - Yes: Guzik says the women were sexually seductive, citing Calvin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-3/ The Geneva notes read "wanton eyes" as a sign they were not chaste. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/3-16.htm
  - No: one Biblical Illustrator writer sees "no reference to immorality," only pride in beauty and clothes. https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/3-16.htm
- **Not an allegory.** The Pulpit Commentary calls an allegorical reading "over-fanciful": these are the women of Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/3-16.htm
- **Background.** JFB and Barnes connect it to the luxury of Uzziah's prosperous reign. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/3-16.htm

### v. 17
- Ellicott: partly diseases of misery and captivity, partly invaders stripping the women of their clothes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-3.html
- The NET Bible renders it "skin diseases" and baldness on the front of the head. https://www.blueletterbible.org/sample/net/isa/3/1/

### vv. 18–23
- **The list.** Ellicott counts twenty-one items, many with foreign-sounding names, and links the passage to 1 Peter 3:3–4 and 1 Timothy 2:9. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-3.html
- **Individual items.** All from Ellicott, same page:
  - The crescents may be linked to the worship of Ashtaroth.
  - The "charms" are amulets against the evil eye.
  - The perfume bottles are literally "houses of the soul."
  - The mirrors were polished metal.
- **"Anklets."** Preceptaustin notes the word is used only once elsewhere (Proverbs 7:22), for fetters, and wonders whether Isaiah intends a double meaning. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_316-23_commentary
- **Application.** Henry: God notices the vanity of proud women, even in their dress, and wasting time and money while neglecting piety and justice displeases Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/3-16.htm

### v. 24
- Ellicott: the stench of squalor; the rope used to drag captives; the shaved heads of slaves; a brand on the flesh marking them as their captors' property. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-3.html

### vv. 25–26
- The Pulpit Commentary says the mention of warriors falling makes plain that the judgment will be an invasion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/3-2.htm
- Ellicott and JFB both compare Zion sitting on the ground to the "Judaea Capta" coins Rome struck after Titus destroyed Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-3.html and https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Isa/Isa_003.cfm
